<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_bibliography"><a href="#bib" title="In Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">References</span></a></li>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Moo Jin Kim</span>    <span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Chelsea Finn</span>    <span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Percy Liang<a href="https://openvla-oft.github.io" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium" style="font-size:120%;">https://openvla-oft.github.io</a></span>
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent vision-language-action models (VLAs) build upon pretrained vision-language models and leverage diverse robot datasets to demonstrate strong task execution, language following ability, and semantic generalization. Despite these successes, VLAs struggle with novel robot setups and require fine-tuning to achieve good performance, yet how to most effectively fine-tune them is unclear given many possible strategies. In this work, we study key VLA adaptation design choices such as different action decoding schemes, action representations, and learning objectives for fine-tuning, using OpenVLA as our representative base model. Our empirical analysis informs an Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe that integrates parallel decoding, action chunking, a continuous action representation, and a simple L1 regression-based learning objective to altogether improve inference efficiency, policy performance, and flexibility in the model’s input-output specifications. We propose OpenVLA-OFT, an instantiation of this recipe, which sets a new state of the art on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, significantly boosting OpenVLA’s average success rate across four task suites from 76.5% to 97.1% while increasing action generation throughput by 26<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>. In real-world evaluations, our fine-tuning recipe enables OpenVLA to successfully execute dexterous, high-frequency control tasks on a bimanual ALOHA robot and outperform other VLAs (<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and RDT-1B) fine-tuned using their default recipes, as well as strong imitation learning policies trained from scratch (Diffusion Policy and ACT) by up to 15% (absolute) in average success rate.
We release code for OFT and pretrained model checkpoints at <a href="https://openvla-oft.github.io" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://openvla-oft.github.io</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/figure_1_openvla_aloha.001.jpeg" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/249;" width="429" height="249" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 1: </span><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT+ on the bimanual ALOHA robot.</span> Our Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe enhances fine-tuned OpenVLA policies through improved inference efficiency, model quality, and input-output flexibility. The resulting OpenVLA-OFT+ policies execute diverse dexterous manipulation tasks on a real-world bimanual robot at high control frequencies (25 Hz). The “+” suffix indicates the integration of feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, which strengthens language grounding in tasks where accurate language understanding is critical for success.</figcaption>
</figure><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span><sup id="footnotex1.1" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>Stanford University.
Correspondence to:
Moo Jin Kim <a href="mailto:moojink@cs.stanford.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;moojink@cs.stanford.edu&gt;</a>,
Chelsea Finn <a href="mailto:cbfinn@cs.stanford.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;cbfinn@cs.stanford.edu&gt;</a>,
Percy Liang <a href="mailto:pliang@cs.stanford.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;pliang@cs.stanford.edu&gt;</a>.
</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent vision-language-action models (VLAs)—robot policies built by fine-tuning pretrained vision-language models on large-scale robot datasets for low-level robotic control—have demonstrated strong task performance, semantic generalization, and language following abilities across diverse robots and tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. Despite their strengths, fine-tuning is crucial for satisfactory deployment of VLAs on novel robots and tasks, yet it is unclear what the most effective approach for adaptation is given the large design space. A robotics practitioner who wishes to fine-tune a VLA to a new robot setup and task may default to using the same training recipe used for pretraining (or a parameter-efficient variant), but it is not obvious whether this would yield the best policy, and there is limited empirical analysis of alternative fine-tuning approaches in the literature.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work has begun exploring VLA adaptation strategies, with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [22]</a></cite> proposing parameter-efficient fine-tuning via LoRA. However, their autoregressive action generation remains too slow (3-5 Hz) for high-frequency control (25-50+ Hz), and both LoRA and full fine-tuning of autoregressive VLAs often yield unsatisfactory performance in bimanual manipulation tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. While recent approaches improve efficiency through better action tokenization schemes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>, achieving 2 to 13<math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedups, significant latency between action chunks (e.g., 750 ms for the recent FAST approach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>) still limits real-time deployment on high-frequency bimanual robots. Exploring alternative VLA adaptation approaches that achieve both satisfactory speed and quality remains an underexplored area of research.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we study key design decisions for adapting VLAs to novel robots and tasks using OpenVLA, a representative autoregressive VLA, as our base model. We examine three key design choices: action decoding scheme (autoregressive vs. parallel generation), action representation (discrete vs. continuous), and learning objective (next-token prediction vs. L1 regression vs. diffusion). Our study reveals several key insights that build on each other: (1) parallel decoding with action chunking not only boosts inference efficiency but also improves success rates on downstream tasks while enabling greater flexibility in the model’s input-output specifications; (2) continuous action representations further improve model quality compared to discrete representations; and (3) fine-tuning the VLA with an L1 regression objective yields comparable performance to diffusion-based fine-tuning while offering faster training convergence and inference speed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Building on these insights, we introduce <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT</span>: an instantiation of an Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe that integrates parallel decoding and action chunking, continuous action representations, and an L1 regression objective to enhance inference efficiency, task performance, and model input-output flexibility while maintaining algorithmic simplicity. We conduct experiments on both the standardized LIBERO simulation benchmark and dexterous tasks on a real bimanual ALOHA robot. In LIBERO, OpenVLA-OFT establishes a new state of the art by achieving 97.1% average success rate across four task suites, outperforming both fine-tuned OpenVLA policies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> (76.5%) and <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> policies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> (94.2%) while achieving a 26<math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup in action generation with 8-step action chunks. For real-world ALOHA tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, we augment our recipe with FiLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> for enhanced language grounding, denoting the augmented recipe as <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OFT+</span>. OpenVLA-OFT+ successfully executes dexterous bimanual tasks like folding clothes and manipulating target food items based on the user’s prompt (see Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), outperforming both fine-tuned VLAs (<math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and RDT-1B) and prominent imitation learning policies trained from scratch (Diffusion Policy and ACT) by up to 15% (absolute) in average success rate. With 25-timestep action chunks, OpenVLA-OFT+ achieves 43<math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster throughput than base OpenVLA, demonstrating that our new fine-tuning recipe enables real-time robot control with strong task performance and language following ability.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/ar_vs_pr--cont_vs_discr--v2.001.jpeg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/75;" width="476" height="75" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 2: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Key design decisions for VLA fine-tuning.</span> <span id="S1.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left</span>: Comparison between autoregressive decoding, which generates actions sequentially, and parallel decoding, which leverages bidirectional attention and generates all actions in a single forward pass. <span id="S1.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right</span>: Comparison between discrete action tokens with next-token prediction and continuous action values with L1 regression or diffusion modeling objectives. The original OpenVLA training scheme includes autoregressive decoding, discrete actions, and next-token prediction.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Work</span></h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior works have leveraged language and vision foundation models to enhance robotic capabilities, utilizing them as pretrained visual representations that accelerate robotic policy learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, for object localization in robotics tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, and for high-level planning and reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. More recently, researchers have explored fine-tuning vision-language models (VLMs) to directly predict low-level robotic control actions, producing “vision-language-action” models (VLAs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, which have demonstrated effective generalization to out-of-distribution test conditions and unseen semantic concepts. These works focus primarily on model development, while we focus on developing a recipe for fine-tuning such models, justifying individual design decisions with insights that we gain from our empirical analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the importance of fine-tuning for real-world VLA deployment, empirical analysis of effective fine-tuning recipes remains limited. While <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [22]</a></cite> study various parameter update strategies and from their findings show that LoRA fine-tuning enables effective adaptation to single-arm robots operating at low control frequencies (<math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;10</annotation></semantics></math> Hz), their analysis does not extend to bimanual robots with high control frequencies (25-50+ Hz), a more complex control scenario. We address this gap by exploring VLA adaptation design decisions for fast inference and reliable task execution on a real-world bimanual manipulator with a 25 Hz controller.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recent works by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belkhale and Sadigh [2]</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pertsch et al. [36]</a></cite> improve VLA efficiency through new action tokenization schemes, using vector quantization or discrete cosine transform-based compression to represent action chunks (sequences of actions) with fewer tokens than simple per-dimension binning (as used in RT-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> and OpenVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>). While these approaches achieve 2 to 13<math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedups for autoregressive VLAs, we explore design decisions beyond autoregressive modeling, which remains inherently limited by iterative generation. Our parallel decoding approach, when paired with action chunking, achieves significantly greater speedups: 26<math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> to 43<math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> throughput with much lower latency (0.07 ms for single-arm tasks with one input image and 0.321 ms for bimanual tasks with three input images).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Another line of research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> demonstrates effective VLA fine-tuning for high-frequency, bimanual manipulation using generative approaches like diffusion or flow matching. While these diffusion-based VLAs achieve higher action throughput than autoregressive VLAs by generating multi-timestep action chunks simultaneously, they introduce computational trade-offs through slower training and multiple denoising or integration steps at inference time. Furthermore, these diffusion VLAs vary considerably in architecture, learning algorithm, vision-language fusion approach, and input-output specifications—and which design elements most significantly impact performance remains unclear. Through controlled experiments, we show that policies fine-tuned with a simpler L1 regression objective can match more complex approaches in task performance while achieving significantly greater inference efficiency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Preliminaries</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Original OpenVLA formulation.</span> We use OpenVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> as our representative base VLA, a 7B-parameter manipulation policy created by fine-tuning the Prismatic VLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> on 1M episodes from the Open X-Embodiment dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>. See Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A-A Model Architecture Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A-A</span></a> for architecture details. OpenVLA’s original training formulation uses <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">autoregressive</span> prediction of 7 <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">discrete</span> robot action tokens per timestep: 3 for position control, 3 for orientation control, and 1 for gripper control. It employs <span id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">next-token prediction</span> with cross-entropy loss as its learning objective, similar to language models. We explore alternative formulations including parallel decoding, continuous action representations, and learning objectives like L1 regression and diffusion modeling in the next few sections.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action chunking.</span> Prior works have shown that action chunking—i.e., predicting and executing a sequence of future actions without intermediate replanning—improves policy success rates across many manipulation tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. However, OpenVLA’s autoregressive generation scheme makes action chunking impractical, as generating even a single-timestep action takes 0.33 seconds on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. For a chunk size of <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> timesteps and action dimensionality <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>, OpenVLA requires <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="KD" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">KD</annotation></semantics></math> sequential decoder forward passes versus just <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> passes without chunking. This <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-fold increase in latency makes action chunking impractical for high-frequency robots under the original formulation. In the next section, we present a parallel generation scheme that enables efficient action chunking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Studying Key VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions</span></h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first outline key design decisions for adapting VLAs to novel robot setups and tasks and provide details on their implementation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing approaches that fine-tune VLAs using the base model’s autoregressive training recipe face two key limitations: slow inference speed (3-5 Hz) unsuitable for high-frequency control, and unreliable task execution on bimanual manipulators <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we investigate three key design components for VLA fine-tuning:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action generation strategy (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, left):</span> We compare autoregressive generation, which requires sequential token-by-token processing, with parallel decoding, which generates all actions simultaneously and enables efficient action chunking.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action representation (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, right):</span> We examine discrete actions (256-bin discretization of normalized actions) processed through softmax-based token prediction, versus continuous actions directly generated by an MLP action head. For discrete actions, the final hidden states of the language model decoder are linearly projected into logits, which are processed by a softmax operation to form the probability distribution over action tokens. For continuous actions, the final hidden states are instead mapped directly to normalized continuous actions by a separate action head MLP.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning objective (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, right):</span> We compare policies fine-tuned with next-token prediction for discrete actions, L1 regression for continuous actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, and conditional denoising diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> for continous actions (similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi et al. [5]</a></cite>).</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct our study using OpenVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> as the base model, adapting it via LoRA fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> due to our relatively small training datasets (500 demonstrations versus 1M demonstrations for pretraining).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Implementing Alternative Design Components</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The base OpenVLA model originally employs autoregressive generation of discrete action tokens optimized via next-token prediction. We implement alternative design decisions for fine-tuning while keeping the original pretraining unchanged. We describe the key implementation aspects below, with further details explained in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A-B Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A-B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parallel decoding and action chunking.</span> Unlike autoregressive generation which requires sequential token prediction, parallel decoding enables the model to map input embeddings to the predicted output sequence in a single forward pass. We modify the model to receive empty action embeddings as input and replace the causal attention mask with bidirectional attention, allowing the decoder to predict all actions simultaneously. This reduces action generation from <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> sequential passes to a single pass, where <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> is the action dimensionality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Parallel decoding naturally extends to action chunking: to predict actions for multiple future timesteps, we simply insert additional empty action embeddings in the decoder’s inputs, which are then mapped to a chunk of future actions. For chunk size <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, the model predicts <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="KD" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">KD</annotation></semantics></math> actions in one forward pass, increasing throughput <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-fold with minimal latency impact. While parallel decoding may theoretically be less expressive than autoregressive approaches, our experiments show no performance degradation across diverse tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Continuous action representations.</span> OpenVLA originally uses discrete action tokens where each action dimension is normalized to <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math> and uniformly discretized into 256 bins. While this approach is convenient since it requires no architectural modifications to the underlying VLM, the discretization process can sacrifice fine-grained action details. We study continuous action representations with two learning objectives drawn from prominent imitation learning approaches:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">First, similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. [53]</a></cite>, we implement L1 regression by replacing the decoder’s output embedding layer with an MLP action head that directly maps final decoder layer hidden states to continuous action values. The model is trained to minimize the mean L1 difference between predicted and ground-truth actions, maintaining the efficiency benefits of parallel decoding while potentially improving action precision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Second, inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi et al. [5]</a></cite>, we implement conditional denoising diffusion modeling where the model learns to predict noise added to action samples during forward diffusion. During inference, the policy gradually denoises noisy action samples via reverse diffusion to produce real actions. While this approach offers potentially more expressive action modeling, it requires multiple forward passes during inference (50 diffusion steps in our implementation), impacting deployment latency even with parallel decoding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Additional model inputs and outputs.</span> While the original OpenVLA processes a single camera view, some robot setups include multiple viewpoints and additional robot state information. We implement a flexible input processing pipeline: For camera images, we use OpenVLA’s dual vision encoder to extract 256 patch embeddings per view, which are projected into the language embedding space with a shared projector network. For low-dimensional robot state inputs (e.g., joint angles and gripper state), we employ a separate projection network to map these into the same embedding space as one additional input embedding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">All input embeddings—visual features, robot state, and language tokens—are concatenated along the sequence dimension before being passed to the decoder. This unified latent representation enables the model to attend to all available information when generating actions. Combined with parallel decoding and action chunking, this architecture can efficiently process rich multimodal inputs while generating multiple timesteps of actions, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Augmenting OpenVLA-OFT with FiLM for Enhanced Language Grounding.</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Challenges with language following.</span> When deploying on the ALOHA robot setup with multiple viewpoints including from wrist-mounted cameras, we observe that policies can struggle with language following due to spurious correlations in visual inputs. During training, policies may learn to latch onto such spurious correlations when predicting actions, rather than properly attending to the language instructions, resulting in poor adherence to the user’s commands at test time. Furthermore, language inputs may only be critical at specific moments in a task—for example, after grasping the spoon and deciding which ingredient to scoop in the “scoop X into bowl” task discussed in Section <a href="#S6" title="VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a>. Therefore, without special techniques, training the model to appropriately focus on language inputs can be particularly challenging.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FiLM.</span> To enhance language following, we employ feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, which infuses language embeddings into the visual representations so that the model pays more attention to the language inputs. We compute the average of the language embeddings <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> from the task description and project it to obtain scaling and shifting vectors <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>. These vectors modulate the visual features <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐅</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}</annotation></semantics></math> through an affine transformation:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FiLM}(\mathbf{F}|\mathbf{\gamma},\mathbf{\beta})=\mathbf{\hat{F}}=(1+\mathbf{\gamma})\odot\mathbf{F}+\mathbf{\beta}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>FiLM</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐅</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mi>𝐅</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FiLM}(\mathbf{F}|\mathbf{\gamma},\mathbf{\beta})=\mathbf{\hat{F}}=(1+\mathbf{\gamma})\odot\mathbf{F}+\mathbf{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A crucial implementation detail is the choice of what represents a “feature” for modulation in vision transformers. While one might naturally consider treating individual patch embeddings as features to be modulated, we find that this approach results in poor language following. Instead, drawing from how FiLM operates in convolutional networks, where modulation applies spatially-agnostically by scaling and shifting entire feature maps, we apply each element of <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> to the corresponding hidden unit across all visual patch embeddings so that <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> influence all patch embeddings. Concretely, this makes <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{ViT}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{ViT}</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vectors, where <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{ViT}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{ViT}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of hidden dimensions in visual patch embeddings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We apply FiLM after the self-attention layer and before the feedforward layer in each vision transformer block, with separate projectors for each block (see Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A-C Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A-C</span></a>. We only use FiLM for the ALOHA experiments discussed in Section <a href="#S6" title="VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a>, where multiple camera viewpoints lead to a larger presence of spurious correlations in visual inputs.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Experiments: Evaluating VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions</span></h2>

<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/libero_tasks.001.jpeg" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/324;" width="476" height="324" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 3: </span><span id="S5.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LIBERO simulation benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> task suites.</span> We study VLA fine-tuning design decisions using four representative task suites. Here we depict two of ten tasks per suite.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we evaluate the effects of our proposed VLA adaptation design decisions through controlled experiments aimed at answering three key questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How does each design decision affect the fine-tuned policy’s success rate on downstream tasks?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How does each design decision affect model inference efficiency (action generation throughput and latency)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How do the alternative fine-tuning formulations affect flexibility in model input-output specifications?</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">V-A</span> </span><span id="S5.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LIBERO Experimental Setup</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on the LIBERO simulation benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, which features a Franka Emika Panda arm in simulation with demonstrations containing camera images, robot state, task annotations, and delta end-effector pose actions. We use four task suites—LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Long—each providing 500 expert demonstrations across 10 tasks to assess policy generalization to different spatial layouts, objects, goals, and long-horizon tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [22]</a></cite>, we filter unsuccessful demonstrations and fine-tune OpenVLA via LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> on each task suite independently. We train for 50-150K gradient steps for non-diffusion methods and 100-250K steps for diffusion methods (which converge slower), using a batch size of 64-128 across 8 A100/H100 GPUs. We test checkpoints every 50K steps and report the best performance for each run. Unless specified otherwise, policies receive one third-person image and language instruction as input. For methods using action chunking, we set chunk size to <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=8</annotation></semantics></math> to match the Diffusion Policy baseline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, and execute full chunks before replanning, which we find improves both speed and performance. See Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A-D OpenVLA-OFT Hyperparameters and Training Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A-D</span></a> for hyperparameter details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our primary baseline in this study is the base OpenVLA model fine-tuned using the original fine-tuning recipe. However, for broader comparison, we also include LIBERO results from prior state-of-the-art imitation learning methods, such as Diffusion Policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, Octo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, DiT Policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, Seer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>, MDT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, and <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. Note that Seer uses additional LIBERO-90 pretraining data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE I: </span><span id="S5.T1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LIBERO task performance results.</span> Success rates (SR) across LIBERO benchmark task suites <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. Results include policies fine-tuned from pretrained base models (Octo, DiT Policy, Seer, <math id="S5.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>), models trained from scratch (Diffusion Policy, Seer (scratch), MDT), and OpenVLA variants using different fine-tuning design decisions: parallel decoding (PD), action chunking (AC, chunk size <math id="S5.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=8</annotation></semantics></math> timesteps), and continuous actions with L1 regression (Cont-L1) or with diffusion (Cont-Diffusion). OpenVLA results from this work are averaged over 500 trials for each task suite (10 tasks × 50 episodes). Our full OpenVLA-OFT method with additional inputs achieves state-of-the-art 97.1% average success rate. Baseline results are from the original papers, except for Diffusion Policy, Octo, and the original OpenVLA policies, whose results are reported by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. [22]</a></cite>. Bold and underlined values indicate best and second-best performance.</figcaption>

<tr id="S5.T1.4.1.17" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T1.4.1.17.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_r"><math id="S5.T1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> + FAST (fine-tuned) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite></th>
<td id="S5.T1.4.1.17.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r">96.4</td>
<td id="S5.T1.4.1.17.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r">96.8</td>
<td id="S5.T1.4.1.17.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r">88.6</td>
<td id="S5.T1.4.1.17.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r">60.2</td>
<td id="S5.T1.4.1.17.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">85.5</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T1.4.1.18" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S5.T1.4.1.18.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r"><span id="S5.T1.4.1.18.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">96.8</span></td>

<tr id="S5.T1.4.1.19" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S5.T1.4.1.19.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r"><span id="S5.T1.4.1.19.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">97.6</span></td>

</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">V-B</span> </span><span id="S5.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LIBERO Task Performance Comparisons</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For satisfactory deployment, robot policies must demonstrate reliable task execution. We first assess how different VLA fine-tuning design decisions affect success rates on the LIBERO benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our efficiency analysis (which we discuss later) reveals that parallel decoding (PD) and action chunking (AC) together are necessary for high-frequency control (25-50+ Hz), especially for bimanual robots with double the amount of action dimensions. We therefore evaluate OpenVLA policies with both techniques used jointly, comparing variants using discrete actions, continuous actions with L1 regression, and continuous actions with diffusion.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Results in Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ V-A LIBERO Experimental Setup ‣ V Experiments: Evaluating VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> show that parallel decoding and action chunking not only increase throughput but also improve performance significantly, raising average success rates by 14% (absolute) over autoregressive OpenVLA policies. This improvement is particularly pronounced in LIBERO-Long, suggesting that action chunking helps capture temporal dependencies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> and reduce compounding errors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, which ultimately leads to smoother and more reliable task execution. In addition, we find that using continuous action variants further improves success rates by 5% (absolute) over the discrete action variant, likely due to higher precision in the action predictions. L1 regression and diffusion variants achieve comparable performance, indicating that the high-capacity OpenVLA model can effectively model the multi-task action distribution even with simple L1 regression.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE II: </span><span id="S5.T2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LIBERO inference efficiency results.</span> Action generation throughput and latency for 7-dimensional actions, averaged over 100 queries on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. We compare OpenVLA variants with parallel decoding (PD), action chunking (<math id="S5.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=8</annotation></semantics></math> timesteps), and continuous actions using L1 regression or diffusion objectives. The last row adds wrist camera image and robot state inputs. Bold and underlined values show best and second-best performance.</figcaption>
