</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">V-C</span> </span><span id="S5.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LIBERO Inference Efficiency Comparisons</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Efficient inference is crucial for deploying VLAs on high-frequency control robots. We now evaluate how parallel decoding (PD), action chunking (AC), and continuous action representations affect model inference speed. We measure average latency (time to generate one robot action or action chunk) and throughput (total actions generated per second) by querying each model variant 100 times on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Each query processes a 224 x 224 px image and a sample LIBERO language instruction (“pick up the alphabet soup and place it in the basket”).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Results in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ V-B LIBERO Task Performance Comparisons ‣ V Experiments: Evaluating VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a> show that parallel decoding reduces latency and increases throughput by 4<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> by replacing 7 sequential forward passes through the decoder portion of the policy with a single pass. Adding action chunking (<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=8</annotation></semantics></math>) increases latency by 17% due to longer attention sequences in the decoder, but when combined with parallel decoding, it dramatically improves throughput, achieving a 26<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup over baseline OpenVLA. The continuous actions variant with L1 regression shows negligible difference in efficiency since the additional MLP action head adds minimal computational cost compared to the base model. The diffusion variant requires 50 denoising steps and thus suffers from 3<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> greater latency. However, it still achieves 2<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> higher throughput than baseline OpenVLA through parallel decoding and chunking. This means that despite longer pauses between action chunks, the diffusion variant still completes robot episodes more quickly than the original autoregressive variant.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">V-D</span> </span><span id="S5.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Model Input-Output Flexibility</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As explained in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="IV-B Implementing Alternative Design Components ‣ IV Studying Key VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B</span></a> and validated by our efficiency evaluations in the prior section, parallel decoding enables OpenVLA to generate action chunks with minimal latency increase, thereby enhancing flexibility in model <em id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">outputs</em>. The significant speedup realized by parallel decoding and action chunking creates headroom for processing additional model <em id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">inputs</em> as well. We demonstrate this by fine-tuning OpenVLA with additional inputs such as robot proprioceptive state and a robot wrist-mounted camera image, which doubles the number of visual patch embeddings being passed into the language model decoder, from 256 to 512. Despite this substantial increase in input sequence length, the fine-tuned OpenVLA policy maintains high throughput (71.4 Hz) and low latency (0.112 sec), as shown in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ V-B LIBERO Task Performance Comparisons ‣ V Experiments: Evaluating VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluating these policies with additional inputs on the LIBERO benchmark reveals further improvements in average success rate across all task suites (Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ V-A LIBERO Experimental Setup ‣ V Experiments: Evaluating VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>). Notably, our enhanced fine-tuned OpenVLA policies outperform even the best fine-tuned <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> policies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>—which benefit from a base model with larger-scale pretraining and a more sophisticated learning objective (flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>)—as well as the Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MDT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>. Even with a simpler base model pretrained on less data than more recent VLAs, we find that our alternative VLA adaptation design decisions empower fine-tuned OpenVLA policies to establish a new state of the art on the LIBERO benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS5.6" class="ltx_text">V-E</span> </span><span id="S5.SS5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Optimized Fine-Tuning Recipe</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the demonstrated improvements in task performance, inference efficiency, and model input-output flexibility, we propose an <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT)</span> recipe for VLA adaptation that combines three key components:</p>
<ol id="S5.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">parallel decoding with action chunking</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">continuous action representation</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">L1 regression objective</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These design choices work together to produce strong policies that can be deployed at high frequencies while maintaining algorithmic simplicity. We denote policies fine-tuned from the OpenVLA base model using our OFT recipe as <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT</span>. In Section <a href="#S6" title="VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a>, we evaluate OpenVLA-OFT’s capabilities on dexterous, bimanual manipulation tasks in the real world using a high-frequency control robot.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS6.6" class="ltx_text">V-F</span> </span><span id="S5.SS6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Additional Experiments</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given that the alternative fine-tuning formulation, along with additional model inputs and outputs, induces a distribution shift between the base VLA’s pretraining and fine-tuning, one reasonable question is whether the base VLA’s pretrained representations are helpful and have any influence on the results we have reported. We conduct an ablation study in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS7" title="A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A-G</span></a> to address this question, ablating the OpenVLA pretraining phase and directly fine-tuning the underlying pretrained VLM with the OFT recipe. As shown in Table <a href="#A1.T14" title="TABLE XIV ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">XIV</span></a>, the base OpenVLA pretrained representations are indeed still beneficial for robotic policy learning, as removing them leads to a 5.2% drop in average success rate (absolute) in our LIBERO evaluation suite.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VI </span><span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot</span></h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While our experimental results in the prior section demonstrate OpenVLA-OFT’s effectiveness in simulation, successful deployment in the real world, on robot platforms that differ substantially from those seen during pretraining, is crucial for showing broad applicability. We thus assess the efficacy of our optimized fine-tuning recipe on the ALOHA robot setup <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, a real bimanual manipulation platform operating at a high control frequency. We evaluate on novel dexterous manipulation tasks that have never been encountered before during OpenVLA’s pretraining (which only involves single-arm robot data).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> have shown that vanilla LoRA fine-tuning with autoregressive VLAs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> is impractical for such tasks, as its throughput (3-5 Hz for single-arm robots and even lower for bimanual tasks) falls well below the 25-50 Hz required for real-time deployment. We therefore exclude this baseline from our experiments and compare more effective methods that we discuss shortly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we use an augmented version of our VLA fine-tuning recipe (<span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OFT+</span>) that additionally includes feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) for enhanced language grounding, as described in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Augmenting OpenVLA-OFT with FiLM for Enhanced Language Grounding. ‣ IV Studying Key VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a>. We denote the OpenVLA policy instantiated through this augmented fine-tuning recipe as <span id="S6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT+</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">VI-A</span> </span><span id="S6.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ALOHA Experimental Setup</span></h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The ALOHA platform comprises two ViperX 300 S arms, three camera viewpoints (one top-down, two wrist-mounted), and robot state inputs (14-dimensional joint angles). It operates at 25 Hz (reduced from the original 50 Hz to enable faster training while still maintaining smooth robotic control), with actions representing target absolute joint angles. This setup differs significantly from OpenVLA’s pretraining, which includes single-arm robot data only, a single camera viewpoint from a third-person camera, no robot state inputs, low-frequency control (3-10 Hz), and relative end-effector pose actions. The distribution shift poses a challenge to the adaptation of this model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We design four representative tasks testing deformable object manipulation, long-horizon skills, tool usage, and language-driven control:</p>
<ol id="S6.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“fold shorts”</span>: Fold white shorts on a table with two consecutive bimanual folds. Training: 20 demonstrations. Evaluation: 10 trials.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“fold shirt”</span>: Fold white T-shirt through multiple synchronized bimanual folds, testing contact-rich, long-horizon manipulation. Training: 30 demonstrations. Evaluation: 10 trials.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“scoop X into bowl”</span>: Move bowl to center of table with left arm, scoop specified ingredient (“raisins,” “almonds and green M&amp;Ms,” or “pretzels”) with right arm using metal spoon. Training: 45 demonstrations (15 per ingredient). Evaluation: 12 trials (4 per ingredient).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“put X into pot”</span>: Open pot with left arm, place specified item (“green pepper,” “red pepper,” or “yellow corn”) with right arm, close pot. Training: 300 demonstrations (100 per object). Evaluation: 24 trials (12 in-distribution, 12 out-of-distribution).</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We fine-tune OpenVLA using OFT+ on each task independently for 50-150K gradient steps (total batch size 32 with 8 A100/H100-80GB GPUs) with action chunk size <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=25</annotation></semantics></math>. At inference time, we execute the full action chunk before requerying the model for the next chunk.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">VI-B</span> </span><span id="S6.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Methods in Comparison</span></h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The ALOHA tasks present a significant adaptation challenge for OpenVLA as the base model, given the substantial differences from its pretraining platforms in terms of control frequency, action space, and input modalities. For this reason, we compare OpenVLA-OFT+ against more recent VLAs—RDT-1B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> and <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>—that were pretrained on bimanual manipulation data and might reasonably be expected to perform better on these downstream tasks. We evaluate these models after fine-tuning them using their authors’ recommended recipes, and these methods serve as important points of comparison. Additionally, to provide comparisons with computationally efficient alternatives, we evaluate two popular imitation learning baselines: ACT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> and Diffusion Policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, trained from scratch on each task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To enable language following in these baseline methods, we use language-conditioned implementations. For ACT, we modify EfficientNet-B0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> to process CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> language embeddings via FiLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">*</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">*</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">*</span>
              
              
              
            We use this FiLM-EfficientNet implementation only for language-dependent tasks (“scoop X into bowl” and “put X into pot”). For clothes folding tasks, we use the original ResNet-18 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> backbone as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span> For Diffusion Policy, we use the DROID dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> implementation that conditions action denoising on DistilBERT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> language embeddings, modified to support bimanual control and multiple image inputs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/aloha_task_performance_results_v2.001.jpeg" id="S6.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/163;" width="429" height="163" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 4: </span><span id="S6.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ALOHA task performance results.</span> Comparison between policies trained from scratch (ACT, Diffusion Policy) and fine-tuned VLAs (RDT-1B, <math id="S6.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, OpenVLA-OFT+) across four ALOHA manipulation tasks. OpenVLA-OFT+ enhances the base model with parallel decoding, action chunking, continuous actions, L1 regression, and FiLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> for language grounding. Fine-tuned VLAs consistently outperform from-scratch methods, with OpenVLA-OFT+ achieving the highest average performance.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S6.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/aloha_language_grounding_results.001.jpeg" id="S6.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/159;" width="476" height="159" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 5: </span><span id="S6.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ALOHA language following results.</span> Success rates in approaching language-specified target objects for language-dependent tasks. Fine-tuned VLAs follow the user’s command more frequently than policies trained from scratch. OpenVLA-OFT+ shows the strongest language grounding, though removing FiLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> reduces success to chance level.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">VI-C</span> </span><span id="S6.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ALOHA Task Performance Results</span></h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate all methods—ACT, Diffusion Policy, RDT-1B, <math id="S6.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, and OpenVLA-OFT+—on our four ALOHA tasks. To provide fine-grained assessment, we use a predetermined rubric that assigns scores for partial task completion (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS6" title="A-F ALOHA Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A-F</span></a> for details). Figure <a href="#S6.F4" title="Fig. 4 ‣ VI-B Methods in Comparison ‣ VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows aggregate performance scores, while Figure <a href="#S6.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ VI-B Methods in Comparison ‣ VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> specifically tracks language following ability for the language-dependent tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance of non-VLA baselines.</span> The baseline methods trained from scratch show varying levels of success. ACT, while able to complete basic tasks, produces less precise actions and achieves the lowest overall performance. Diffusion Policy demonstrates stronger capabilities, matching or exceeding RDT-1B’s reliability on the clothes folding and scooping tasks. However, it struggles with the “put X into pot” task which has a larger training dataset, suggesting limited scalability compared to VLA-based approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance of fine-tuned VLAs.</span> Fine-tuned VLA policies generally outperform the from-scratch baselines in both task execution and language following, consistent with prior findings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. Among VLAs, we observe distinct characteristics: RDT-1B achieves good language following through its “Alternating Condition Injection” scheme <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, but shows a limitation in handling closed-loop feedback. As visualized in Figure <a href="#S6.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ VI-D ALOHA Inference Efficiency Comparisons ‣ VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, it often fails to correct mistakes in the “scoop X into bowl” task—for instance, continuing to pour ingredients into an imaginary bowl after missing the actual bowl, suggesting over-reliance on proprioceptive state over visual feedback. On the other hand, <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> demonstrates more robust execution with smoother motions and better reactivity to feedback, often successfully recovering from initial failures (as shown in Figure <a href="#S6.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ VI-D ALOHA Inference Efficiency Comparisons ‣ VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). While its language following slightly trails RDT-1B’s, <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> achieves better overall task completion, making it the strongest baseline. Finally, OpenVLA-OFT+ achieves the highest performance across both task execution and language following (see Figure <a href="#S6.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ VI-D ALOHA Inference Efficiency Comparisons ‣ VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> for examples of successful task rollouts). This is particularly noteworthy given that the base OpenVLA model was pretrained only on single-arm data, while RDT-1B and <math id="S6.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> were pretrained on substantial bimanual datasets (6K episodes and 8K hours of bimanual data, respectively). This suggests that the fine-tuning technique can be more crucial than pretraining data coverage for downstream performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation study of FiLM.</span> We evaluate the importance of FiLM in our OpenVLA-OFT+ approach by ablating it and assessing the policies’ language following ability on the last two tasks, which require good language grounding for successful execution. As shown in Figure <a href="#S6.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ VI-B Methods in Comparison ‣ VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, language following drops to 33% in both tasks—equal to randomly choosing the correct instruction. This demonstrates that FiLM is essential for preventing the model from overfitting to spurious visual features and ensuring proper attention to language inputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Please see the project website for ALOHA robot rollout videos and an in-depth qualitative analysis of all methods: <a href="https://openvla-oft.github.io" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://openvla-oft.github.io</a></p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE III: </span><span id="S6.T3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ALOHA robot inference efficiency results.</span> Throughput and latency measurements averaged over 100 queries on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Each query processes three 224 × 224 px images, 14-D robot state, and a task command (“scoop raisins into bowl”). All methods use action chunk size K=25, except Diffusion Policy (K=24, as a multiple of 4 is required) and the original OpenVLA (K=1, no chunking). RDT-1B predicts 64 actions, but we execute the first 25 only for fair comparison. </section>
<section id="S6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">VI-D</span> </span><span id="S6.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ALOHA Inference Efficiency Comparisons</span></h3>

<figure id="S6.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/openvla_rollouts.001.jpeg" id="S6.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:452/473;" width="452" height="473" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 6: </span><span id="S6.F6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sample successful OpenVLA-OFT+ rollouts on the ALOHA robot.</span> OpenVLA-OFT+ can fold clothes, use a metal spoon to scoop and pour targeted trail mix ingredients into a bowl, and place targeted objects into a pot. See <a href="https://openvla-oft.github.io" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">our website</a> for videos.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S6.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/rdt_pi0_rollouts.001.jpeg" id="S6.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/501;" width="476" height="501" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 7: </span><span id="S6.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sample rollouts contrasting RDT-1B and <math id="S6.F7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> error handling in ALOHA tasks.</span> <span id="S6.F7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top</span>: In some cases, RDT-1B fails to respond to missed bowl placement, continuing to pour ingredients into empty space. <span id="S6.F7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom</span>: <math id="S6.F7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> demonstrates adaptive behavior by reattempting green pepper grasp after initial failure, highlighting better visual feedback integration. See <a href="https://openvla-oft.github.io" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">our website</a> for videos.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate inference efficiency by measuring action generation throughput and latency across 100 queries for each method. We report the results in Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ VI-C ALOHA Task Performance Results ‣ VI Experiments: Adapting OpenVLA to a Real-World ALOHA Robot ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>. The original OpenVLA formulation, even with just the additional wrist camera inputs, shows poor efficiency with 1.8 Hz throughput and 0.543 sec latency. In contrast, OpenVLA-OFT+ achieves 77.9 Hz throughput, though its latency is higher compared to the policies in the prior LIBERO experiments since it must process two additional input images.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Other methods demonstrate higher throughput than OpenVLA-OFT+ due to their smaller architectures: ACT (84M parameters), Diffusion Policy (157M), RDT-1B (1.2B), and <math id="S6.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> (3.3B)—while OpenVLA has 7.5B parameters. ACT achieves the highest speed by combining L1 regression-based single-pass action generation (like OpenVLA-OFT+) with its compact architecture. Also, despite its larger size, <math id="S6.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> outperforms both RDT-1B and Diffusion Policy in speed thanks to its optimized JAX implementation (all other methods are implemented in PyTorch).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Notably, OpenVLA-OFT+’s throughput (77.9 Hz) approaches RDT-1B’s (84.1 Hz) despite being 7<math id="S6.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger, as it generates actions in a single forward pass rather than requiring multiple denoising steps as in RDT-1B.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VII </span><span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Discussion</span></h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our study on VLA fine-tuning design decisions reveals how different components impact inference efficiency, task performance, model input-output flexibility, and language following ability. These insights lead to our Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe, which enables effective VLA adaptation to novel robots and tasks through parallel decoding, action chunking, continuous actions, L1 regression, and (optionally) FiLM language conditioning. The success of OFT is particularly noteworthy with OpenVLA: despite having no exposure to bimanual robots or multi-view image inputs during pretraining, OpenVLA fine-tuned with OFT can adapt to such configurations and match or even outperform more recent diffusion-based VLAs (<math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> and RDT-1B) which <em id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">have</em> encountered bimanual manipulators and multiple input images during pretraining. This demonstrates that a well-designed fine-tuning recipe can have a significant impact on final performance, and existing VLAs can be successfully adapted to new robotic systems without extensive retraining from scratch. Moreover, our results show that a simple L1 regression-based approach with a high-capacity model such as OpenVLA is quite effective for adapting to novel robots and tasks. This approach offers practical advantages over diffusion-based methods: the simpler algorithm leads to faster training convergence and inference speed while maintaining strong performance, making it particularly suitable for real-world robotics applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VIII </span><span id="S8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Limitations</span></h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While our Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe shows promise for adapting VLAs to novel robots and tasks, several important questions remain.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Handling multimodal demonstrations.</span> Our experiments use focused demonstration datasets with a consistent strategy per task. While L1 regression may help smoothen out noise in training demonstrations by encouraging the policy to learn the median mode in demonstrated actions, it may struggle to accurately model truly multimodal action distributions where multiple valid actions exist for the same input, which may not be ideal in cases where the ability to generate alternative action sequences would be beneficial for task completion. Conversely, diffusion-based approaches may better capture such multimodality but risk overfitting to suboptimal modes in training data (see <a href="https://openvla-oft.github.io/#l1-regression-vs-diffusion" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">our website</a> for discussions and video illustrations of these nuances). Understanding OFT’s effectiveness with multimodal demonstrations remains an important direction for future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pretraining versus fine-tuning.</span> Our study focuses specifically on <em id="S8.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fine-tuning</em> VLAs for downstream tasks. Whether OFT’s benefits extend effectively to <em id="S8.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pretraining</em>, or whether more expressive algorithms like diffusion are necessary for large-scale training, requires further investigation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inconsistent language grounding.</span> Our ALOHA experiments reveal that OpenVLA without FiLM exhibits poor language grounding, despite showing no such issues in LIBERO simulation benchmark experiments. The source of this discrepancy—whether from the lack of bimanual data in pretraining or other factors—remains unclear and warrants further study.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Appendix</h2>

<figure id="A1.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.19645v1/fig/film_figure.001.jpeg" id="A1.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/243;" width="476" height="243" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 8: </span><span id="A1.F8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) implementation in OpenVLA’s vision backbone.</span> We integrate FiLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> into both SigLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> and DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> vision transformers in OpenVLA’s fused vision backbone. The average task description embedding modulates visual features through scale and shift operations at each transformer block, enhancing language-vision integration. This modification significantly improves language following in ALOHA tasks.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="A1.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">A-A</span> </span><span id="A1.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Model Architecture Details</span></h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Base OpenVLA Architecture.</span> OpenVLA combines a fused vision backbone (with both SigLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> and DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> vision transformers), a Llama-2 7B language model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, and a 3-layer MLP projector with GELU activation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> for projecting visual features into the language embedding space.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The original model processes a single third-person image and a language instruction (e.g., “put eggplant into pot”). The fused vision encoder extracts 256 patch embeddings from each vision transformer, concatenates them along the hidden dimension, and projects them into the language embedding space. These projected features are concatenated with language embeddings along the sequence dimension before being processed by the Llama-2 decoder to output a 7-dimensional robot action representing delta end-effector pose, represented by a string of discrete action tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT architecture modifications.</span> OpenVLA-OFT introduces six key changes:</p>
<ol id="A1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">processes multiple input images (e.g., third-person image plus wrist camera images) through the shared SigLIP-DINOv2 backbone</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">projects robot proprioceptive state to language embedding space via a 2-layer MLP with GELU activation</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">replaces causal attention with bidirectional attention for parallel decoding</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">substitutes the language model decoder output layer with a 4-layer MLP (ReLU activation) for generation of continuous actions (instead of discrete actions)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">5.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">outputs chunks of K actions instead of single-timestep actions</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">6.</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">(for OpenVLA-OFT+) adds FiLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> modules that use the average task language embedding to modulate visual features in both SigLIP and DINOv2 vision transformers (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A-C Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A-C</span></a> for details)</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The complete OpenVLA-OFT+ architecture is illustrated in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="A1.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">A-B</span> </span><span id="A1.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Implementation Details</span></h3>

<section id="A1.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">A-B</span>1 </span>Parallel Decoding Implementation</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the original OpenVLA autoregressive training scheme, the model receives ground-truth action tokens shifted right by one position as input (a setup known as teacher forcing). A causal attention mask ensures the model only attends to current and previous tokens. At test time, each predicted token is fed back as input for the next prediction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For parallel decoding, we replace this input with empty action embeddings that differ only in their positional encoding values (similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>). We also use a bidirectional attention mask (instead of causal), enabling the model to leverage all intermediate features non-causally when predicting each element in the action chunk.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS2.6" class="ltx_text">A-B</span>2 </span>Continuous Action Representations</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For discrete actions, increasing the number of bins used for discretization improves precision but reduces the frequency of individual tokens in the training data, potentially hurting generalization. On the other hand, with a continuous action representation, the VLA can directly model the action distribution without lossy discretization.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our continuous representation implementations use the following specifications:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">L1 regression:</span> The MLP action head consists of 4 layers with ReLU activation, mapping final Llama-2 decoder layer hidden states directly to continuous actions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diffusion:</span> We use:</p>
<ul id="A1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DDIM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> sampler with 50 diffusion timesteps</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Squared cosine beta schedule following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">4-layer noise predictor with same MLP architecture as the L1 regression head</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="A1.SS2.SSS3.6" class="ltx_text">A-B</span>3 </span>Input Processing Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Passing each input image through the OpenVLA fused vision encoder produces 256 patch embeddings, which are projected to the langauge model embedding space via a 3-layer MLP with GELU activation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. Low-dimensional robot states are also projected to the language embedding space through a 2-layer MLP with GELU activation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="A1.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">A-C</span> </span><span id="A1.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) Implementation Details</span></h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FiLM schematic.</span> Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Augmenting OpenVLA-OFT with FiLM for Enhanced Language Grounding. ‣ IV Studying Key VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a> describes how we implement feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> for OpenVLA. Figure <a href="#A1.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> illustrates our implementation. OpenVLA has a fused vision encoder with both SigLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> and DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> vision transformers, and we apply FiLM to both transformers.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Design considerations.</span> In our implementation, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al. [35]</a></cite>, we multiply <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐅</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1+\mathbf{\gamma})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1+\mathbf{\gamma})</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> since <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> are near zero at initialization. This helps preserve the visual encoder’s original activations at the start of fine-tuning, minimizing perturbation in the pretrained representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation specifics.</span> The functions <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> that project language embeddings to obtain <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> are implemented as simple affine transformations. Separate projectors are learned for each transformer block to allow for block-specific modulation patterns. This design enables the model to learn different modulation patterns at different levels of visual feature processing.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">One might initially consider modulating each patch embedding independently, as opposed to each hidden dimension of each embedding as discussed in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Augmenting OpenVLA-OFT with FiLM for Enhanced Language Grounding. ‣ IV Studying Key VLA Fine-Tuning Design Decisions ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a>. However, our spatially-agnostic modulation approach more closely mirrors FiLM’s operation in convolutional networks, where modulation applies globally across spatial dimensions since entire feature maps are scaled and shifted by individual elements of <math id="A1.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>. This design choice better maintains the benefits of FiLM and improves the policy’s language grounding substantially. We find that an alternative formulation that modulates each patch embedding independently leads to weaker language grounding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="A1.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">A-D</span> </span><span id="A1.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">OpenVLA-OFT Hyperparameters and Training Details</span></h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT training details for LIBERO.</span> Hyperparameters for OpenVLA-OFT fine-tuning on LIBERO are listed in Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="TABLE IV ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a>. We train until the mean L1 loss between predicted and ground-truth normalized actions (scaled between <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-1,+1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-1,+1]</annotation></semantics></math>) falls below 0.01. For faster convergence, we decay the learning rate from 5e-4 to 5e-5 after 100K gradient steps. We evaluate checkpoints every 50K steps, with the 150K checkpoint achieving best performance in all task suites except for LIBERO-Goal. Note that we do not use FiLM for LIBERO experiments since the fine-tuned policies without it already demonstrate good language grounding.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT+ training details for ALOHA.</span> Hyperparameters for OpenVLA-OFT+ training on ALOHA tasks (with FiLM in the augmented OFT+ recipe) are shown in Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="TABLE V ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V</span></a>. We maintain the same convergence criterion as in the LIBERO experiments (training until mean noramlized L1 loss falls below 0.01) and similar learning rate decay strategy (again 10<math id="A1.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> reduction, but after 50K gradient steps instead of 100K, since the ALOHA datasets are smaller). For the two clothes folding tasks which do not require language grounding, we still include FiLM to verify that these additional parameters do not impair task execution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="A1.SS5.6" class="ltx_text">A-E</span> </span><span id="A1.SS5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Baseline Methods Hyperparameters and Training Details</span></h3>

<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ACT training details for ALOHA.</span> Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="TABLE VI ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a> lists hyperparameters for ACT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> trained from scratch on each task. For non-language-dependent tasks (“fold shorts”, “fold shirt”), we use the default ResNet-18 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> backbone, which does not include language conditioning. For language-dependent tasks (“scoop X into bowl”, “put X into pot”), we implement EfficientNet-B0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> with FiLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>. While the authors of ACT recommend training for at least 5K epochs, we extend training to 10K-70K epochs per task to improve performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diffusion Policy training details for ALOHA.</span> For Diffusion Policy training, we use the DROID implementation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, which conditions action predictions on DistilBERT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> language embeddings of the task description. We list hyperparameters in Table <a href="#A1.T7" title="TABLE VII ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VII</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RDT-1B training details for ALOHA.</span> Hyperparameters for RDT-1B fine-tuning are shown in Table <a href="#A1.T8" title="TABLE VIII ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VIII</span></a>. The authors of RDT-1B recommend training for 150K gradient steps, but we observe that training converges in significantly fewer steps since our fine-tuning datasets are much smaller than the RDT-1B fine-tuning dataset. Therefore, we observe that it is unnecessary to train for such a large amount of time. In fact, on “scoop X into bowl”, the earlier 18K step checkpoint (73.3% success) outperforms the later 40K step checkpoint (70.0%) (we report the former in our ALOHA experiments).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A1.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A1.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> training details for ALOHA.</span> Table <a href="#A1.T9" title="TABLE IX ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IX</span></a> lists hyperparameters for <math id="A1.SS5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> fine-tuning. We use full fine-tuning (the default option in their codebase) and train until convergence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="A1.SS6.6" class="ltx_text">A-F</span> </span><span id="A1.SS6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ALOHA Evaluation Details</span></h3>

<section id="A1.SS6.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="A1.SS6.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">A-F</span>1 </span>ALOHA Task Suite Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Below are detailed specifications for each task in our ALOHA experiments:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1. “fold shorts”</span></p>
<ul id="A1.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Task: Bimanual folding of white shorts with two synchronized folds</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Dataset: 20 demonstrations (19 training, 1 validation)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Episode length: 1000 timesteps (40 seconds)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I3.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluation: 10 trials</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I3.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Initial states: See Figure <a href="#A1.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2. “fold shirt”</span></p>
<ul id="A1.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Task: Long-horizon T-shirt folding with multiple synchronized bimanual folds</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

<li id="A1.I4.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

</div></li>
<li id="A1.I4.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<p id="A1.I4.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluation: 10 trials</p>
</div></li>

<p id="A1.I4.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Initial states: See Figure <a href="#A1.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3. “scoop X into bowl”</span></p>
<ul id="A1.I5" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I5.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Task: Move bowl to center, scoop specified ingredient (raisins, almonds and green M&amp;Ms, or pretzels) into bowl</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I5.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I5.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I5.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Dataset: 45 demonstrations (15 per target; 42 training, 3 validation)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I5.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I5.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I5.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Episode length: 900 timesteps (36 seconds)</p>
</div></li>

<div id="A1.I5.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I5.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluation: 12 trials</p>

<li id="A1.I5.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I5.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I5.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Initial states: See Figure <a href="#A1.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS6.SSS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4. “put X into pot”</span></p>
<ul id="A1.I6" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I6.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I6.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I6.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Task: Open pot, place specified item (green pepper, red pepper, or yellow corn) into pot, close pot</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I6.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I6.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I6.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Dataset: 300 demonstrations (100 per target; 285 training, 15 validation)<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">†</span>
                      
                      
                      
                    This relatively large number of demonstrations for the “put X into pot” task is not necessary for satisfactory performance. It simply reflects an earlier investigative phase of this work during which we encountered difficulties with language grounding in learned policies and initially hypothesized that increasing demonstration quantity might improve language following capabilities. However, merely expanding the training set proved insufficient for achieving satisfactory language grounding, and we discovered that additional techniques were needed for more reliable language grounding. We still decided to fine-tune on the full dataset with 300 demonstrations nonetheless.</span></span></span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I6.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I6.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I6.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Initial variation: 45 cm horizontal, 20 cm vertical for food items; fixed pot pose</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I6.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I6.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I6.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Episode length: 400 timesteps (16 seconds)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I6.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I6.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I6.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Evaluation: 24 trials (12 in-distribution evaluations, 12 out-of-distribution evaluations)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I6.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I6.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I6.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Initial states: See Figures <a href="#A1.F12" title="Fig. 12 ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> (in-distribution) and <a href="#A1.F13" title="Fig. 13 ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> (out-of-distribution)</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="A1.SS7.6" class="ltx_text">A-G</span> </span><span id="A1.SS7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Additional Experiments</span></h3>

<div id="A1.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablating the OpenVLA pretrained representation.</span> We evaluate the performance of OpenVLA-OFT policies produced by fine-tuning the underlying Prismatic VLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> directly on the LIBERO downstream datasets without OpenVLA’s Open X-Embodiment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> robot pretraining. This ablation study investigates whether OpenVLA’s robot-pretrained representation remains valuable when subjected to a substantially different fine-tuning approach such as OFT. The results in Table <a href="#A1.T14" title="TABLE XIV ‣ A-G Additional Experiments ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">XIV</span></a> demonstrate that the variant without the pretrained OpenVLA representation consistently underperforms compared to the full OpenVLA-OFT model, confirming the benefits of using the pretrained representation for downstream policy learning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE IV: </span><span id="A1.T4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OpenVLA-OFT hyperparameters for LIBERO.</span> We specify the hyperparameters for the full OpenVLA-OFT approach which includes parallel decoding, action chunking, continuous actions with L1 regression, and additional inputs (wrist camera and robot state).</figcaption>

<th id="A1.T8.4.13.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">use proprio (robot state)</th>
<td id="A1.T8.4.13.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">yes</td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T8.4.14" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T8.4.14.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row"># trainable parameters</th>
<td id="A1.T8.4.14.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">1.2B</td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T8.4.15" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T8.4.15.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">diffusion sampling algorithm</th>
<td id="A1.T8.4.15.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">DDPM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> at train time; DPM-Solver++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> at test time</td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T8.4.16" class="ltx_tr">

<tr id="A1.T8.4.17" class="ltx_tr">

</tbody>
